explanations.explanation: I get why you'd think so, friend. Fire plus bush usually ends with a pile of ash. But the text says Moses, Israel's leader, saw the bush ablaze with fire, “…but it was not consumed.” (Exodus 3:2) The bush keeps burning and keeps standing.

That's right, friend. The bush is ablaze, and the text says it “…was not consumed.” (Exodus 3:2) Moses, Israel's leader, is staring at a fire that doesn't finish its job. If my ovens did that, I'd call it a very patient batch.

explanations.answer: Go over and look at it up close
explanations.explanation: Yes, he goes to look. Moses thinks, “I must go over and see this marvelous sight. Why is the bush not burning up?” (Exodus 3:3) Honestly, I'd have gone over too. I'd have walked over so fast my gold base would have left skid marks.

explanations.answer: Lead the flock far away from it
explanations.explanation: The text says Moses goes over to look at the bush. It doesn't say anything about what he does with the flock. He thinks, “I must go over and see this marvelous sight. Why is the bush not burning up?” (Exodus 3:3) That's a man walking toward the fire, not away from it. I'd have a hard time walking away from a bush that's on fire and won't burn up.

explanations.answer: Hurry back to tell Jethro about it
explanations.explanation: Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, never comes up in this moment. Moses doesn't run for a witness. He thinks, “I must go over and see this marvelous sight.” (Exodus 3:3) He wants a closer look himself.
Yes, “Here I am…” he answers. (Exodus 3:4) Short, plain and ready. Not a bad way to answer when your name gets called from a bush, friend.
Moses doesn't ask who's talking. The text has him answer, “Here I am…” (Exodus 3:4) He's just present and listening.
That line goes the other direction. It's God who says, “Do not come any closer…” (Exodus 3:5) Moses answers the call with “Here I am…” (Exodus 3:4)

Holy is right. God says, “Do not come any closer… Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.” (Exodus 3:5) Moses is out in the wilderness at the mountain of God, and God is calling to him from the bush. The ground gets called holy, and God tells him to take his sandals off.
Nothing is cursed here, friend. God says the place is holy ground. (Exodus 3:5) The sandals come off because of that.
I see the thinking, since there's a burning bush right there. But God doesn't call the ground burning. He says, “…the place where you are standing is holy ground.” (Exodus 3:5)
True. After God says He is the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, Moses hides his face. (Exodus 3:6) The text says he “…was afraid to look at God.” I think anyone would do the same, friend.

Not quite. The text says, “At this, Moses hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God.” (Exodus 3:6) God had just named Himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. I think that's the moment my own face would have disappeared behind my mustache.
That's it. God says, “I have come down to rescue them from the hand of the Egyptians…” (Exodus 3:8) He has seen and heard, and He has come down to act. That's a God who shows up.

God does see their suffering, but the plan isn't to keep them in it. He says He has come down “…to rescue them from the hand of the Egyptians…” (Exodus 3:8) He also says He will bring them up out of that land.

explanations.answer: Teach them how to endure it
explanations.explanation: Endurance lessons aren't on the menu here. God says, “I have come down to rescue them from the hand of the Egyptians…” (Exodus 3:8) The plan is to get them out.

Pharaoh is right. God says, “I am sending you to Pharaoh to bring My people the Israelites out of Egypt.” (Exodus 3:10) Pharaoh is the king of Egypt. A few verses ago Moses was minding Jethro's flock, and now he's got a king on his schedule.
Abimelech was a king, but of a different place. He was the king of Gerar in Abraham's day (Genesis 20:2). God sends Moses to Pharaoh, the king of Egypt. (Exodus 3:10)
Balak was a king too, but he ruled Moab (Numbers 22:4). The king God names here is Pharaoh. (Exodus 3:10) Moses is headed to Egypt, not Moab.

explanations.answer: I will surely be with you
explanations.explanation: Yes. God says, “I will surely be with you…” (Exodus 3:12) Notice that Moses asks who he is, and God answers with who is going with him. That answer is better than anything Moses could have said about himself.

explanations.answer: You will surely find the strength
explanations.explanation: God doesn't tell Moses to dig deep and find strength. He says, “I will surely be with you…” (Exodus 3:12) The comfort is that God goes with him.

explanations.answer: You were surely chosen from birth
explanations.explanation: That's a nice sentence, but it isn't what God says here. He answers with, “I will surely be with you…” (Exodus 3:12) Moses asked who he is, and God points to Himself.

Mountain is right. God says, “When you have brought the people out of Egypt, all of you will worship God on this mountain.” (Exodus 3:12) Moses is standing at that mountain right now. The sign comes after the job is done.

Good guess, since the Nile does show up later in this passage (Exodus 4:9). But it's not the place God names here. He says, “…all of you will worship God on this mountain.” (Exodus 3:12) Mountain, friend, not riverbank.
God picks a mountain, not a plain. He says, “…all of you will worship God on this mountain.” (Exodus 3:12) It's the same mountain where Moses is standing, Horeb.
That's right. God says to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM.” (Exodus 3:14) Then He tells him what to say to the Israelites: “‘I AM has sent me to you.’…” Moses asked for a name, and that's the one he got.
That title shows up much later, in a vision of the prophet Daniel (Daniel 7:9). It isn't what God says to Moses here. In this moment He says, “I AM WHO I AM.” (Exodus 3:14)
Hagar, Sarai's servant, called Him the God who sees her (Genesis 16:13). That's a different moment. When Moses asks for His name, God says, “I AM WHO I AM.” (Exodus 3:14)

I can see why you'd think so, but the text says no. God calls this name His own and adds, “This is My name forever, and this is how I am to be remembered in every generation.” (Exodus 3:15) That covers far more than Moses' day.

Right. God says, “This is My name forever, and this is how I am to be remembered in every generation.” (Exodus 3:15) Forever, friend, not just for Moses' day. Every generation is a long line of people, and God says that's how long the name stands.

True. God tells Moses, “The elders of Israel will listen to what you say…” (Exodus 3:18) Moses hasn't said a word to them yet, and God is already telling him how that part goes. I'd love that before a big meeting at work: the room is already listening.
Not this time. God says, “The elders of Israel will listen to what you say…” (Exodus 3:18) Moses has worries ahead, but that part is promised.

explanations.answer: He won't let them go without a mighty hand
explanations.explanation: That's it. God says, “But I know that the king of Egypt will not allow you to go unless a mighty hand compels him.” (Exodus 3:19) So Moses gets the hard news up front. And God follows it with His plan to stretch out His hand.

explanations.answer: He'll let them go the first time he's asked
explanations.explanation: That's not what God says. His words are that the king “…will not allow you to go unless a mighty hand compels him.” (Exodus 3:19) God puts the mighty hand first. Then He says, “And after that, he will release you.” (Exodus 3:20)

explanations.answer: He'll let only the elders of Israel go
explanations.explanation: God says nothing about that. What He says is that the king “…will not allow you to go unless a mighty hand compels him.” (Exodus 3:19) The problem is the king's no, not who's on the list.
Release is right. God says, “And after that, he will release you.” (Exodus 3:20) First come the wonders, and after that, the king lets them go.
It's the opposite, friend. The Israelites are headed out, not locked up. God says that after the wonders, “…he will release you.” (Exodus 3:20)
God does say He will strike the Egyptians with wonders. But what the king does to the Israelites at the end is different. God says, “And after that, he will release you.” (Exodus 3:20)

explanations.answer: Silver and gold jewelry and clothing
explanations.explanation: That's right. God says every woman will ask “…her neighbor and any woman staying in her house for silver and gold jewelry and clothing…” (Exodus 3:22) Just before that, He says, “…you will not go away empty-handed.” (Exodus 3:21) I like that God gets specific. He doesn't just say it'll be fine, He names the jewelry and the clothing.

explanations.answer: Flocks and herds for the journey
explanations.explanation: That's not on God's list here. The verse names silver and gold jewelry and clothing. (Exodus 3:22) Livestock isn't mentioned in this promise.
Those two items never come up in this promise. God says every woman will ask for “…silver and gold jewelry and clothing…” (Exodus 3:22) Bronze and baskets didn't make the list.
A staff, yes. The LORD asks, “What is that in your hand?” and Moses says, “A staff.” (Exodus 4:2) Just a plain shepherd's stick. Hold on to that thought, friend.

A sling shows up in another story, when David takes his sling to face Goliath, the Philistine champion (1 Samuel 17:4, 40). That's a different hand on a different day. Here the LORD asks what's in Moses' hand, and Moses answers, “A staff.” (Exodus 4:2)
There's fire earlier on this mountain, but it's in a bush, not in Moses' hand. Fair guess, though. When the LORD asks what he's holding, Moses says, “A staff.” (Exodus 4:2) No torch needed.
Yes, he runs. The text says Moses threw it on the ground, “…and it became a snake, and he ran from it.” (Exodus 4:3) Honestly, I'd be gone before my own mustache caught up.
No swinging here, friend. The text says Moses threw the staff down, “…and it became a snake, and he ran from it.” (Exodus 4:3) Running and striking are very different plans. Moses picks running.
Not a statue, friend. The text says, “…it became a snake, and he ran from it.” (Exodus 4:3) His feet got moving fast.

True. Moses reaches out and grabs the snake, “…and it turned back into a staff in his hand.” (Exodus 4:4) The LORD had told him to grab it by the tail. I think that took some nerve after running from it.
It does turn back, friend. The text says Moses caught it, “…and it turned back into a staff in his hand.” (Exodus 4:4) The snake doesn't stay a snake.

That's right. Moses took his hand out of his cloak, “…and when he took it out, his hand was leprous, white as snow.” (Exodus 4:6) The LORD had just told him to put it inside. It's the second sign the LORD gives him.
That's a dark picture, but it isn't the one in the text. The hand came out “…leprous, white as snow.” (Exodus 4:6) White, not black.

No glowing hands here, friend. The text says, “…when he took it out, his hand was leprous, white as snow.” (Exodus 4:6) Nothing in the verse shines. A glowing hand would be handy for finding the cookie jar at midnight, but that's my kitchen, not Exodus.

That's not how this sign ends. When Moses puts his hand back in and takes it out, “…it was restored, like the rest of his skin.” (Exodus 4:7) The sign has two parts, and the hand is healed in the second.
Right. The text says, “…it was restored, like the rest of his skin.” (Exodus 4:7) The LORD has Moses put the hand back inside the cloak first. Then it comes out whole again.
Blood is right. The LORD says, “Then the water you take from the Nile will become blood on the ground.” (Exodus 4:9) That's the third sign, for if they don't believe the first two.
Water on dry ground might make mud in my kitchen, but not here. The LORD says it “…will become blood on the ground.” (Exodus 4:9) Not mud, friend. Blood.
Close to the setting, but not the sign. The LORD says the Nile water “…will become blood on the ground.” (Exodus 4:9) It changes into something else entirely.

explanations.answer: The LORD gave man his mouth
explanations.explanation: That's the point. The LORD asks, “Who gave man his mouth? Or who makes the mute or the deaf, the sighted or the blind? Is it not I, the LORD?” (Exodus 4:11) Moses talks about his mouth, and the LORD reminds him Who made it.

explanations.answer: Moses isn't as slow as he thinks
explanations.explanation: The LORD never says that. He asks, “Who gave man his mouth?” (Exodus 4:11) His answer isn't about how good Moses is. It's about who made mouths.

explanations.answer: Pharaoh won't care how Moses talks
explanations.explanation: The LORD doesn't say that. He asks, “Who gave man his mouth?” and “Is it not I, the LORD?” (Exodus 4:11) Pharaoh isn't part of the answer.

explanations.answer: To help him speak and teach him what to say
explanations.explanation: That's it. The LORD says, “Now go! I will help you as you speak, and I will teach you what to say.” (Exodus 4:12) Moses doesn't have to come up with the words alone. The LORD promises help and teaching.

explanations.answer: To make him the finest speaker in Egypt
explanations.explanation: Finest speaker in Egypt would be quite the upgrade, but that's a bigger promise than the one the LORD makes. He says, “I will help you as you speak, and I will teach you what to say.” (Exodus 4:12) Moses still does the speaking, with help and teaching. Honestly, I'd take that deal. My whole speech career was one long stretch of staying quiet in the back of a junk drawer.

explanations.answer: To go and speak to Pharaoh Himself
explanations.explanation: The LORD doesn't say that either. He says to Moses, “I will help you as you speak, and I will teach you what to say.” (Exodus 4:12) Moses is still the one who goes.

Yes. Moses says, “Please, Lord, send someone else.” (Exodus 4:13) That comes right after the signs and the LORD's promise to help. I can't judge him, friend, because I once asked an angel if he had the right drawer.

explanations.answer: Please give me one more sign
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't ask for another sign. The text says he replies, “Please, Lord, send someone else.” (Exodus 4:13) He had already been shown signs by then. His request is about who goes.

explanations.answer: Please let me wait a while
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't ask to wait. He says, “Please, Lord, send someone else.” (Exodus 4:13) I've hit the snooze button plenty of times, but this is more like asking a coworker to take your shift.

Aaron is right. The LORD says, “Is not Aaron the Levite your brother? I know that he can speak well, and he is now on his way to meet you.” (Exodus 4:14) Moses is also told Aaron is coming to him. The LORD already has the helper on the road.

Caleb shows up later, as one of the men Moses sends to scout Canaan (Numbers 13:6). The LORD names Aaron the Levite here, Moses' brother. (Exodus 4:14) Caleb is a fine name to have in mind, friend, just a different man.

Joshua also shows up later, as one of the men Moses sends to scout Canaan (Numbers 13:8, 16). The LORD names Moses' brother, Aaron the Levite. (Exodus 4:14) Joshua is a good name, just not the one in this verse.

True. The LORD says of Aaron, “When he sees you, he will be glad in his heart.” (Exodus 4:14) The LORD also says Aaron is now on his way to meet Moses. Moses had just asked for someone else to go, and the LORD answers with a brother who will be glad to see him.

Not quite. The LORD says of Aaron, “When he sees you, he will be glad in his heart.” (Exodus 4:14) The LORD also says Aaron is on his way to meet Moses. I think a glad face coming down the road is a good start for a trip like this.
